At the University of Zurich, anatomist
Frank Ruhli is studying the remains of
2000 individuals, to help him discover
how the human body has changed over
the last few thousand years, thanks to the
way society has developed and
progressed. Some bones in his collection
show the ravages of diseases that have
long since been eradicated. The modem
way of life, however, continues to
transform not only our waistline but also
our height, muscles and hormones.
_ Some transformations could be genetic
in origin, but there is reason to suspect
others are temporary ones that would
melt away if we returned to & Stone Age
environment. The sheer scale of the
changes shows the ease with which the
human body can adapt to new habitats
over short timescales.
Discovering how those adaptations
make us more vulnerable to certain
diseases is an important facet of
evolutionary medicine, an emerging
specialty that views health through the
lens of evolutionary theory. This
approach sheds light on many common
ailments that have arisen.
The idea that evolution could have
been taking place in the past few
thousand years goes against the
traditional view. Weren't we taught that
natural selection operates over millions of
years? Yet recent evidence indicates

By comparing them with modern-day

Perhaps the best-known difference
our calorie-rich diet and less active
lifestyle. Obviously, that change would be
reversed if we returned to hunting our
food. Another trend is that we have been
becoming less muscular. Bones that no
longer support large muscles can
themselves become weaker, so our
shrinking musculature can be tracked in
the fossil record. Our bones have become
‘gracile’, meaning the overall diameter
has shrunk and the dense outer cortex
has thinned. Christopher Ruff, of Johns
Hopkins University in the USA, has
x-rayed about 100 fossil leg bones, and
examined bones dating back to 3 million
years ago. Ruff's team documented an
average fall in bone strength of 15 per
cent between 2 million and 5000 years
ago. At that point, however, the trend
accelerated, with another 15 per cent
reduction over a mere 4000 years. Ruff

suggests that we retain our ancient
capacity for strength. In turn, stronger
bones mean fewer fractures. Broken hips,
for example, were less common in the
past and are rare in archaeological
specimens, even accounting for the fact
that lives were shorter.
There are other physical changes.
Some of us seem to have acquired a new
blood vessel in our arms, called the
median artery. In fact, this blood vessel is
present in the embryo but it normally
vanishes around the eighth week of
pregnancy, to be replaced by the ulnar
and radial arteries. An increasing number
of adults now retain this artery, Up from
10 per cent at the beginning of the 20th
century to 30 per cent at the end. Ruhli's
former teacher, Maciej Henneberg, is
helping document this change. It could be
due to differences in the diet of pregnant
mothers, he speculates, or modern
medicine.
It is this kind of uncertainty that leaves
some doctors unimpressed with
evolutionary medicine. We cannot know if
evolutionary explanations are true, since
we rarely have a complete picture of the
past, points out American family
physician Harriet Hall. ‘Conventional
medicine has a long record of successes,’
she says. ‘Evolutionary medicine hasn't
proven it has any real value.’ That's not
to say that documenting trends over time
genetic changes have occurred. The point
about these changes is that although they
help protect people from malaria, they
also lead to a higher risk of developing
anaemia, a serious disease which affects
the blood. By studying ancient bodies,
Riihli’s team could narrow down the
window in time when the genetic
alterations arose.
